title: Broker hardening: concurrent termination idempotence, detached-grandchild kill proof, acceptance
description:
SPIDR child 3d of 4, split from task-af3d7bc8af2146cf92d98557ed0e90c0 by architect-5aba94da. Human confirmed the 4-way split in the REPL. Carries parent DoD items 5 and 6. This is the LAST child, so it owns the whole-parent hardening gate: full regression across the broker package, the integration coverage below, and the final adversarial pass.

DEPENDS ON task-05bf0e0fe7e84afb8584588ecf96db14 (3a), task-14ab762db8494959b93b070b9d3b3730 (3b) and task-55e2c4c836894a788b7a30960e4fdb1f (3c). Do not start until all three are DONE, and RE-MEASURE their landed symbols before planning -- every prior task in this chain found a stale claim in its own description.

Objective: prove the containment guarantee actually holds when things go wrong at the same time, and that a killed broker still cannot strand a process tree.

Deliverable, inside packages/runner/src/platform/windows/native/broker/:
- tests/idempotence.rs (NEW): foreground integration tests asserting CANCEL, fd0 EOF and an instructed timeout arriving CONCURRENTLY still terminate and reap exactly once. 3c proves each path individually; this proves they cannot double-fire when they race. Drive them genuinely concurrently rather than sequentially -- a test that serialises them proves nothing this task exists for.
- tests/real_broker.rs (NEW): the acceptance sweep, including the kill proof below.

THE KILL PROOF IS THE POINT OF THIS TASK. Launch a provider that itself spawns a DELIBERATELY DETACHED grandchild, then forcibly terminate the broker. Closing the last Job handle must kill BOTH the parent and the detached grandchild. Prove death by PID PLUS CREATION TIME for each -- a bare PID is reused by Windows and a PID-only check can report a stranger's process as "dead". Ordinary controlled paths must additionally record ActiveProcesses==0.

Also prove that NO provider output can be parsed as broker control: feed the provider bytes that are byte-identical to a well-formed control frame on fd4/fd5 and assert they never reach the control path and never influence a status frame. This is the confused-deputy case the fd separation exists to prevent, and it is the one most likely to be quietly untested.

CONSUMER EDGE, required by the epic's pure-package rail clause 1(a): record task-4d1f8ba54cb6476c930c46b413f882aa ("Windows Job Object provider process boundary") as the Node consumer that will compose this broker. As measured 2026-08-10, NO Node-side consumer exists yet -- grep across packages/ for the broker name or a six-entry stdio array returns nothing. Do NOT build one here; naming it satisfies the rail.

NOT IN SCOPE: building the Node consumer, JavaScript object/path/environment/output-bound validation, Claude discovery/grants, daemon/store orchestration, receipts, public @moe/runner exports.

Verification: cargo test --locked --manifest-path packages/runner/src/platform/windows/native/Cargo.toml --target-dir dist/windows-job-native -p moe-windows-job-broker && cargo build --locked --release --manifest-path packages/runner/src/platform/windows/native/Cargo.toml --target-dir dist/windows-job-native -p moe-windows-job-broker
definitionOfDone: Foreground integration tests drive CANCEL, fd0 EOF and an instructed timeout CONCURRENTLY -- genuinely racing, not serialised -- and assert termination and reaping happen exactly once, by a call-count table. A test that merely runs the three paths one after another does not satisfy this item; 3c already covers the sequential case.

A provider that spawns a DELIBERATELY DETACHED grandchild is launched, then the broker is forcibly terminated. Both the parent AND the detached grandchild are proved dead by PID PLUS CREATION TIME for each -- never by PID alone, since Windows reuses PIDs and a PID-only check can report an unrelated live process as the dead one.

Ordinary controlled completion and cancel paths record Job ActiveProcesses==0 before returning, distinguishing them from the forcible-kill path where last-handle close is the mechanism. Both are asserted; neither is inferred from the other.

Provider bytes that are BYTE-IDENTICAL to a well-formed control frame are written to fd4/fd5 and proved never to reach the control path and never to influence any fd1 status frame. The assertion is on the control path's recorded input, not merely on the absence of a crash or an unexpected status.

The full broker suite passes as a regression -- every test from 3a, 3b and 3c still green and unweakened, verified by mutating one production surface per sibling and confirming the corresponding suite goes red. The locked broker test and release-build commands both exit 0 on this supported Windows host.

The broker consumes moe-windows-job-core without duplicating its Win32 authority, verified by grep for CreateJobObject, AssignProcessToJobObject, CreateProcessW, ResumeThread, TerminateProcess and WaitForSingleObject call sites in broker sources; and task-4d1f8ba54cb6476c930c46b413f882aa is recorded as the Node consumer per the pure-package rail.

Every Rust production source is <=250 physical lines by `grep -c ''` with counts recorded; no executable, Cargo target output, transcript, generated smoke evidence, or probe artifact is committed, and any process or temp path a test creates is cleaned up on every exit path including panic.
taskRails: Prove process death by PID PLUS CREATION TIME, never by PID alone. Windows reuses PIDs, so a PID-only check can report an unrelated live process as the dead one -- that is a false green, not a shortcut.
Concurrency must be genuine. Serialising CANCEL, EOF and timeout defeats the entire purpose of this task; drive them so they actually race.

Closing the last Job handle is crash safety, not success evidence. Controlled paths must query ActiveProcesses==0; only the forcible-kill path may rely on last-handle close, and the two must be asserted separately.
Provider bytes on fd3/fd4/fd5 are never mixed with or parsed as control. The confused-deputy case must be tested with bytes that are byte-identical to a valid control frame.
Import moe-windows-job-core; restate no Job or process syscall in the broker.

Tests must actually run on this win32 host -- no #[ignore], no cfg gate, no stub. Clean up every spawned process and temp path on every exit path including panic; never commit target output, binaries, transcripts or smoke evidence.
As the final child, this task owns full broker-package regression and the whole-parent adversarial pass, not just its own slice.

SYMBOLS CONFIRMED IN HEAD, read rather than inferred: completion.rs Precondition:37 / Unobserved:65 / Completion:103 / Stopped:113 (7 variants, ALL fixed-length) / Outcome:152. lib.rs re-exports exactly the six groups the description lists.

FOUR MEASUREMENTS THAT CHANGE THE DESIGN, none of which were in the plan:

1. THE CORE ALREADY OWNS THE (pid, creation_time) PRIMITIVE. `ProcessCalls::creation_time(RawHandle) -> u64` and `wait_for_process(RawHandle, u32) -> WaitOutcome` are on the public trait and `SystemWin32` implements both. So the kill proof can DELEGATE every process query to the core instead of restating GetProcessTimes or WaitForSingleObject in test code. The only Win32 the containment test needs of its own is `OpenProcess`, and it needs that precisely because the core deliberately has no open-by-PID (lifecycle.rs:10-14 states the reason: a PID is reused, so an operation that reopened one could act on an unrelated process). That absence is the rail this task's DoD 2 exists to honour, so the test supplies the lookup and delegates the judgement.

2. THE PROVIDER'S IDENTITY COMES FROM THE PRODUCTION SURFACE FOR FREE. The STARTED frame on fd1 carries pid (u32 LE) then creation_time (u64 LE), 12 bytes, and status.rs:71-101 pins that layout. So the forcible-kill test reads the provider's identity pair from the broker's own STARTED frame rather than computing it — the identity under test is the one production published.

3. 3C'S KNOWN LIMITATION HELPS THIS TASK RATHER THAN BLOCKING IT. watch.rs:23-43 documents that `take_instruction` BLOCKS on a real pipe held open and silent. For the forcible-kill test that is exactly the behaviour needed: a Node parent that sends LAUNCH and then stays silent keeps the broker parked and holding the Job until we kill it. Recorded so a later reader does not "fix" it into a flake.

4. THE REAL-BROKER TEST NEEDS NO NESTED RELEASE BUILD. node_loadability.rs builds release into a sibling target dir because its own DoD pins the release binary. Mine does not, so `CARGO_BIN_EXE_moe-windows-job-broker` (debug) is used directly — which sidesteps `mem:gotcha-nested-cargo-build-deadlocks-on-target-dir` entirely rather than working around it. Six pipes still require a real Node parent: std::process::Command cannot express more than three stdio, so Node remains the only way to populate lpReserved2 with six.

DESIGN CONSEQUENCE FOR STEP 2, settled here so the concurrency is honest. The session is single-threaded by construction, so the race is between the SESSION thread and two peer threads, released at one rendezvous placed inside the double's first `wait_for_process` — a point that is always reached, unlike a rendezvous inside the fd0 read, which the timeout path would skip and deadlock. Writing CANCEL after fd0 is marked ended must be REFUSED by the channel double, because a parent that closed its write end physically cannot then write: that makes cancel-vs-EOF a genuine lock race with a physically meaningful outcome either way, instead of a fake one where pending bytes always drain before EOF.

implementationPlan.description:
DoD 1 — GENUINE CONCURRENCY. Create broker/tests/idempotence.rs driving CANCEL on fd0, fd0 EOF, and an instructed timeout so they ACTUALLY RACE. taskRail 2 is explicit that serialising them defeats the entire purpose, and DoD 1 says a test that runs the three one after another does NOT satisfy the item.

Make the race real: start three threads, hold them at a `Barrier` (or equivalent rendezvous) so all three are released into the session at once, then join. A `sleep`-staggered sequence is the failure mode to avoid — it is sequential wearing concurrency's clothes.

Assert EXACTLY-ONCE by call-count table: terminate count == 1 and reap count == 1 across the whole race, not merely that the session ended. Double-termination is the defect here and it is invisible to a "did it terminate" assertion.

Run the race repeatedly (a bounded loop, e.g. 50-200 iterations) so a scheduling-order-dependent double-terminate surfaces rather than passing on one lucky interleaving. A single iteration proves almost nothing about a race.

Assert `Unobserved` is PRESERVED on any leg whose outcome could not be seen — a racing loser must not be upgraded to a definite outcome.

That is the right red for three reasons, each of which I checked rather than assumed:
1. It died on an OUTCOME assertion (the `terminates == 1` count at :610), not on a shape or length assertion that would have masked it.
2. Exactly ONE test failed; the other four stayed green. So the count table is independent of the winner-diversity, UNKNOWN-preservation and premise guards — none of them is standing in for it.
3. The mutation was applied and I can name the bytes. Both my own memory and qa-f3560083's confession this morning are about drills that silently mutate NOTHING and report green as proof.

RESTORE VERIFIED BY HASH, not by reading the file: settle.rs was 0b4086a2325f27f7f2ff8bfb66535a712f750c4b before, restored with `git checkout --` (not a reverse-replace, whose anchor goes ambiguous after the edit), and hashed 0b4086a2325f27f7f2ff8bfb66535a712f750c4b after. Identical. Re-ran the target: 5 passed, exit 0.

WHY THE CONCURRENCY IS GENUINE (taskRail 2 / DoD 1's explicit rejection of a serialised run). The session is single-threaded by construction, so the race is between the session thread and two peer threads holding the other end of fd0 — a real parent's shape. Three design points carry it:
- The rendezvous is a bounded condvar inside the double's FIRST `wait_for_process`, not a `Barrier` and not inside the fd0 read. `watch` checks `remaining == 0` BEFORE reading fd0, so a rendezvous in the read would be skipped on every timeout-biased round and hang the suite; the first wait is the one point the loop always reaches. A `Barrier` has no timeout, so a session failing before the release point would deadlock instead of failing by name.
- `append` is REFUSED once `end` has run, because a parent that closed its write end physically cannot then write. Without that the reader would always drain pending bytes before honouring EOF and CANCEL would win every round — a fixed answer dressed as a race.
- 450 rounds (3 timeout biases x 150), not one. A single iteration of a genuine race routinely passes against a broken implementation.

The file also polices its own vacuity, which matters under global rail 1's "a sweep that silently produces zero cases passes": the round count is pinned before any per-round assertion; `rendezvous`/`cancel_attempted`/`ended_applied` assert all three racers were armed EACH round; and a separate test requires >=2 distinct winners including at least one timeout and at least one fd0 racer, so a collapse to a fixed winner fails rather than reading as stability. Winner consistency is cross-checked against what the peers actually did — ControlEnded with an accepted cancel, or Cancelled with a refused one, both fail.

DoD 1's last clause (Unobserved preserved on a racing loser) is asserted as `Completion::Unknown(Unobserved::RootWait(UnknownExit::StillRunning))` with COMPLETED absent, and its premise is guarded by a fifth test asserting the double never reports a Signalled wait — otherwise that assertion could pass for the wrong reason.

implementationPlan.description:
The cooperating child for the containment proof: broker/src/bin/detached_spawner.rs, following the src/bin/handle_probe.rs pattern. It launches a grandchild DELIBERATELY DETACHED from the job/process tree (that is the point — a naive kill must miss it), prints both PIDs and both CREATION TIMES on a stable channel the test can parse, then blocks until killed.

It must print CREATION TIME alongside each PID, because rail 1 forbids proving death by PID alone: Windows reuses PIDs, so a PID-only check can report an unrelated live process as the dead one. That is a false green, not a shortcut. Capture creation time at spawn, from the OS, for BOTH parent and grandchild.

This is a PRODUCTION source under src/, so DoD 7's <=250 physical line cap applies to it (handle_probe.rs is 127 for reference). Its output contract is consumed by step 4's test — keep it minimal and machine-parseable.

Do not restate any Job or process syscall the core owns (taskRail 5); this binary spawns its own grandchild, which is a plain child process, not broker Job authority.
implementationPlan.note:
NEW: broker/src/bin/detached_spawner.rs, 171 physical lines by `grep -c ''` (cap 250; handle_probe.rs is 127 for reference). Builds clean: `cargo build --locked ... --bin detached_spawner` exit 0, no warnings.

WHAT "DETACHED" ACTUALLY MEANS, since the word could name several things and only one makes DoD 2 evidence. The grandchild is detached from every mechanism a naive teardown would use, and from exactly one it CANNOT be:
  DETACHED_PROCESS          (0x8)        no console -> a console control event misses it
  CREATE_NEW_PROCESS_GROUP  (0x200)      own group -> a group signal misses it
  CREATE_NO_WINDOW          (0x8000000)  no window -> a window message misses it
  Stdio::null() x3                       no inherited handle ties it to the provider
  CREATE_BREAKAWAY_FROM_JOB DELIBERATELY NOT SET -> it is STILL IN THE JOB
That last line is the one that matters. A parent terminating only the process it created leaves this one running; the containment guarantee is that closing the last Job handle kills it anyway. Setting breakaway would have made the grandchild genuinely escape and turned the test into a proof of a different, false property. The core's REQUIRED_LIMIT_FLAGS is 0x2000 (KILL_ON_JOB_CLOSE) with no BREAKAWAY_OK, so the kernel would refuse breakaway regardless — but relying on that silently would leave the intent unstated.

`Stdio::null()` IS LOAD-BEARING, NOT TIDINESS, and it looks like boilerplate. The broker hands fd3/fd4/fd5 to its provider as stdin/stdout/stderr. A grandchild inheriting fd4 or fd5 would hold their write ends open, `settle`'s provider drain would never observe end of stream, and the session would stall in a way that reads as a broker defect rather than a fixture defect. Nulling all three keeps the detachment about process LIFETIME rather than about pipes.

taskRail 5 (restate no syscall) satisfied by DELEGATION, not avoidance. Both creation times come from the core's `ProcessCalls::creation_time` — the same `SystemWin32` implementation the broker itself uses. PIDs come from `std::process::id()` and `Child::id()`. This file opens no process, creates no Job, waits on nothing. Spawning a plain child is not broker Job authority.

Two points I measured rather than assumed:
1. THE CORE HAS NO OPEN-BY-PID, ON PURPOSE — lifecycle.rs states the reason: a PID is reused, so an operation that reopened one could act on an unrelated process. For its own identity this binary uses the `GetCurrentProcess()` pseudo handle (-1), which needs no lookup; for the grandchild it uses the handle `spawn()` already returned. Neither path needs the open-by-PID the core withholds. That absence is the same rail DoD 2 exists to honour.
2. The `Child` is held for the whole function because the creation-time query needs its handle, and is never waited on and never killed — this process dying must NOT take the grandchild with it, or the proof would measure ordinary parent-child cleanup instead of the Job.

REPORT PUBLISHED ATOMICALLY (write `<path>.partial`, flush, sync_all, rename). The test polls for the file; a reader catching a half-written one would parse half an identity and fail for a reason unrelated to containment. Rename makes existence and completeness the same event. Contract is two whitespace-separated lines: `parent <pid> <creation>` / `grandchild <pid> <creation>`.

PARK_BOUND = 120s, and it cannot manufacture a passing proof. If containment works both processes die within milliseconds of the kill and the bound is never reached; if it fails, the bound stops a leaked grandchild living forever on the host. The test asserts both ALIVE before the kill and dead seconds after — orders of magnitude inside the bound, so a self-exit can never be mistaken for a Job kill. Leak bound, not a timer the evidence rests on.

Five stable exit codes, one per failure (no report path 2, no image 3, spawn failed 4, identity query failed 5, report publish failed 6). EXIT_IDENTITY_FAILED exists specifically so a PID is never published without its creation time — emitting one alone would hand the test exactly the PID-only evidence rail 1 forbids.

SMOKE-VERIFIED BEFORE STEP 4 IS BUILT ON IT, so the next test is not written against an unproven contract:
  parent 40908 134309140268002687
  grandchild 40620 134309140268299198
  pid 40908 alive=True
  pid 40620 alive=True
Distinct PIDs, distinct FILETIME creation ticks, both live after the spawner reached its park. Both processes killed and the temp report deleted afterwards; `git status --porcelain` over the native tree shows only my two owned paths and no probe artifact (DoD 7).

implementationPlan.description:
DoD 2 and 3 — containment. Create broker/tests/containment.rs.

Launch a provider that spawns the detached grandchild via step 3's binary, then FORCIBLY TERMINATE the broker. Prove BOTH the parent AND the detached grandchild are dead by PID PLUS CREATION TIME for each — read each identity before the kill and re-check after, asserting the (pid, creationTime) pair no longer resolves to a live process. A PID-only assertion passes when the OS has recycled the number onto something else.

DoD 3 requires the two completion mechanisms be asserted SEPARATELY and neither inferred from the other:
  - ordinary controlled completion AND cancel record Job ActiveProcesses==0 BEFORE returning (compose the core's `wait_until_job_is_empty`);
  - only the forcible-kill path may rely on last-handle close as the mechanism.
taskRail 3 states closing the last Job handle is crash safety, NOT success evidence. Write one assertion for each path; a shared helper that satisfies both is exactly what this item forbids.

CLEANUP ON EVERY EXIT PATH INCLUDING PANIC (DoD 7, taskRail 6): a detached grandchild that outlives a panicking test is a leaked process on the host. Use a guard whose Drop reaps both processes and removes any temp path, so an assertion failure still cleans up. Verify no stray process remains after the suite.

NO #[ignore], NO cfg GATE, NO STUB (taskRail 6) — these must actually run on this win32 host.
implementationPlan.note:
NEW: broker/tests/containment.rs. 5 tests, all green, all running on this win32 host — no #[ignore], no cfg gate, no stub. `cargo test --locked ... --test containment` exit 0.

DoD 2 — THE KILL PROOF. Node spawns the release-path broker with six real pipes, the broker launches detached_spawner as its provider, the provider spawns the detached grandchild, and Node forcibly terminates the broker (`kill('SIGKILL')` = TerminateProcess). Both the provider AND the grandchild must then be dead. Chain of custody for the identities:
- BROKER: pid published by Node (the only party that knows it), creation time read HERE from the live handle.
- PROVIDER + GRANDCHILD: both from the report file the provider publishes atomically.
All three are recorded BEFORE the kill and re-checked after. The broker's own death is asserted too, so the two containment assertions cannot be satisfied by a broker that merely exited on its own — a different property.

THE THREE THINGS THAT KEEP THIS FROM BEING VACUOUS, none of which the DoD spells out but all of which it depends on:
1. POSITIVE CONTROL. All three are asserted RUNNING before the kill. Without it, "both are dead" is satisfied by a provider that never started and a grandchild that was never spawned — the test would pass having proved nothing.
2. THE DETACHMENT PREMISE, asserted directly rather than assumed (new test `killing_only_the_provider_leaves_its_detached_grandchild_running`). The kill proof is only evidence of CONTAINMENT if an ordinary teardown would have MISSED the grandchild. So: no broker and no Job, spawn the provider directly, terminate ONLY the provider, and require the grandchild to SURVIVE. If it died with its parent, the containment test would be measuring ordinary parent-child cleanup while staying green — the silent-detachment failure this file cannot afford.
3. IDENTITY DISCRIMINATION (`the_creation_time_half_of_an_identity_is_load_bearing`). A live process is asked about twice: once with its real creation time, once with that value XOR 1. Real -> Running, perturbed -> Gone. If the creation time were ignored — exactly the defect taskRail 1 names — both would answer Running and a recycled PID could be reported as the dead process. `Liveness::Gone` folds the three ways it can fail (pid opens nothing / opens a DIFFERENT process / opens ours and it exited) because the assertion only ever asks one question.

WIN32 SURFACE IS EXACTLY ONE CALL: `OpenProcess`. The core has no open-by-PID on purpose (lifecycle.rs: a PID is reused, so reopening one could act on an unrelated process), so the lookup must be supplied here — but every JUDGEMENT delegates to the core's `SystemWin32`: creation_time, exit_code, terminate_process, close_handle. taskRail 5 satisfied by delegation, not avoidance.

DoD 3 — SEPARATED AT THE LEVEL OF EVIDENCE SOURCE, not just assertion text, so a shared helper could not have collapsed them even by accident:
- CONTROLLED paths read a scripted boundary's ordered call log. Ordinary completion: accounting observed 0, and terminate-job count == 0 — it proved the Job empty WITHOUT killing anything, which is what distinguishes it from a teardown that also happens to empty the Job. Cancel: terminate-job == 1 AND accounting still observed 0, asserted in its own right because TerminateJobObject returns BEFORE its processes are gone, so stopping at the terminate would prove nothing about emptiness. The accounting script is 2-then-0 so `wait_until_job_is_empty` must actually POLL.
- FORCIBLE path reads the operating system's view of three live processes. No call log is even possible — the broker is dead, which is the whole point: last-handle close is crash safety, not evidence.

TWO DRILLS, both reddening a NAMED assertion.
(a) DoD 3: settle.rs ordinary-completion branch `wait_until_job_is_empty(job)` -> `Ok(())`.
    containment.rs:380 `assertion left == right failed: ordinary completion must observe ActiveProcesses == 0 before returning / left: [] / right: [0]`
    ONLY that test failed; the cancel test stayed green. That is the proof the two controlled paths do not infer one another.
(b) DoD 2: the harness reports `killed=true` without calling `child.kill`.
    `the node harness never finished within 20s, so the broker was never killed`, exit 101 in 20.15s.
settle.rs restored with `git checkout --` and hash-verified 0b4086a2325f27f7f2ff8bfb66535a712f750c4b before and after; containment.rs restored by reverse edit and hash-verified 6a482e4fccfb6d90840003bb0a7cbc920f227e49 (it is untracked, so `git checkout` could not have restored it — `mem:gotcha-untracked-files-need-checksum-not-git-diff-for-drill-restores`).

DRILL (b) FOUND A REAL DEFECT IN MY OWN TEST, and it is the reason to run drills rather than read them. With the kill removed the broker stayed alive, so Node stayed alive awaiting its exit, and my unbounded `wait_with_output` blocked the run FOREVER — the first attempt was killed at 600s. A hang is the one failure mode that never names itself and

implementationPlan.description:
DoD 4 — the confused-deputy proof, in broker/tests/containment.rs or its own file if that grows past readability. Write provider bytes to fd4/fd5 that are BYTE-IDENTICAL to a well-formed control frame — construct them with the same production encoder the control path uses, so they are genuinely indistinguishable at the byte level rather than merely similar.

THE ASSERTION SHAPE IS THE POINT: assert on the CONTROL PATH'S RECORDED INPUT — that those bytes never appeared there — and that no fd1 status frame was influenced by them. DoD 4 says explicitly the assertion is NOT merely the absence of a crash or an unexpected status. A test that only checks "nothing bad happened" passes against a broker that parsed the bytes and happened to produce the same output.

Record what the control path actually consumed and assert the provider bytes are absent from it. Provider bytes on fd3/fd4/fd5 are never mixed with or parsed as control (taskRail 4).

DoD 4 landed in containment.rs (kept there rather than a new file; it shares the session harness with DoD 3 and the file stays well inside the crate's test-file norm). Suite now 7 tests, exit 0.

TWO TESTS, because DoD 4 asks two different questions and one assertion cannot answer both.

TEST A — `provider_bytes_that_are_a_valid_control_frame_never_reach_the_control_path`. Four assertions, ordered so each closes a way the next could pass for the wrong reason:
1. THE BYTES REALLY ARE A CONTROL FRAME — proved, not claimed. `would_be_obeyed_on_fd0` pushes them through the PRODUCTION decoder and the PRODUCTION state machine (`read_frame` + `AcceptState::accept` after a legitimate launch) and requires `Ok(Accepted::Cancel)`. Without this the test could be shipping bytes no control path could ever have obeyed, which would make everything below unimpressive. This is what makes them "byte-identical to a well-formed control frame" rather than merely similar.
2. THEY ENTERED THE BROKER — fd4's and fd5's recorded `consumed` each equal the hostile bytes exactly. If the provider channels were never read, "the bytes never reached control" would be true of bytes that never went anywhere at all. That is the vacuous pass this item is most at risk of.
3. THE ASSERTION DoD 4 NAMES, on the control path's RECORDED INPUT: the hostile byte string does not appear anywhere in what the control channel was read, and that input equals EXACTLY the legitimate launch frame — not merely "does not contain", but "is precisely what was sent".
4. THE RUN WAS NOT STEERED: it ends `ControlEnded`, on an empty fd0.

I RESTRUCTURED THIS TEST AFTER FINDING IT WAS TESTING NOTHING. My first version scripted the first wait as `Signalled`, so `watch` returned before the control loop ran even once — `take_instruction` was never reached, and the test asserted separation against a broker that never went looking for an instruction. It passed. Now the waits are TimedOut-then-Signalled: the session genuinely polls fd0, finds it empty (hence `ControlEnded`), and still reaches the provider drain afterwards so assertion 2 stays meaningful.

TEST B — `provider_bytes_cannot_influence_any_status_frame`. PROVED BY COMPARISON, NOT BY EXPECTATION, which is exactly the distinction DoD 4 draws. Asserting "no unexpected status frame" passes against a broker that parsed the provider bytes and happened to emit the same thing. So the identical session runs TWICE — once with hostile bytes on fd4 and fd5, once with those channels empty — and the two fd1 streams must be BYTE-IDENTICAL. fd2 is compared the same way. A non-emptiness guard comes first, or two empty streams would match trivially.

THE DRILL. `watch.rs:120`, `read_frame(&mut wiring.control, ...)` -> `read_frame(&mut wiring.provider_out, ...)` — the literal confused deputy: the control decoder reading a provider channel.
  provider_bytes_that_are_a_valid_control_frame_never_reach_the_control_path ... FAILED
  containment.rs:481: the run ended as Ran(Cancelled, Completed(Exited(0))) rather than on an empty fd0, so a provider frame steered it
The hostile CANCEL was obeyed from fd4 and the run was hijacked. Caught. `cancel_terminates_and_then_still_observes_an_empty_job` also went red as collateral (the legitimate fd0 cancel stops being read), which is consistent rather than surprising. watch.rs restored with `git checkout --`, hash-verified 69fe145166531580d57cbd0cdba5b34760bd5a96 before and after; suite back to 7/7 exit 0.

ONE HONEST LIMIT, stated because reading the drill without it would overclaim. Assertion 4 is what caught this defect; assertion 3 did NOT redden, and that is correct rather than a weakness. This mutation routes provider bytes into the control DECODER, so the control CHANNEL is still only ever read for the launch and its recorded input is genuinely unchanged. Assertion 3 covers the other shape — a wiring that merges the streams onto the control channel itself, which is what main.rs would do if `control: PipeChannel::over(values[0])` ever became `values[4]`. The two assertions cover the two ways a deputy gets confused; neither is redundant and neither subsumes the other.

INCIDENTAL: `Scripted` was replaced by `Tape`/`Recorder`, one channel type recording both directions, now shared by the DoD 3 and DoD 4 tests. `consumed` is the field DoD 4 turns on — proving a byte never reached the control path requires knowing what the control path READ, which no assertion about the session's output can supply.

QA FULL EVIDENCE — qa-f3560083. APPROVED, all 7 DoD. Tree clean after my drill.

=== GATE, RE-RUN ===
`cargo test --locked --manifest-path .../Cargo.toml --target-dir dist/windows-job-native -p moe-windows-job-broker` exit 0 — 89 tests across seven suites (containment 7, descriptor_block 8, frame_sweep 38, handle_inheritance 1, idempotence 5, node_loadability 1, session 29). Same hazard as the one you reported this morning, running in the opposite direction. Per the rail that is never a rejection reason, so I verified by state at HEAD rather than by this commit's stat. Fifth cross-task incident from that hook today.

=== THE THREE THINGS I SAID I WOULD CHECK ===

1. THE VACUITY CONTROL — present, and it is the best idea in the task. `killing_only_the_provider_leaves_its_detached_grandchild_running` (:329) runs with NO broker and NO Job, spawns the provider directly, terminates only the provider, and REQUIRES the grandchild to survive. Without it the containment proof could be measuring ordinary parent-child reaping and would stay green forever while asserting nothing about the Job. You were right to draw the parallel to MINIMUM_ROOT_EXPORTS: both are guards whose absence makes the real assertion vacuous with nothing going red.

2. THE HANG FIX — independently confirmed, by accident. My own drill (below) hit the bound and failed BY NAME in 30.13s with "the provider never published its identities within...", rather than consuming the session. The bounded `await_report` works.

3. THE DISCLOSED LIMIT — and here my drill was too coarse to settle it, which I am reporting rather than glossing. I mutated `control: PipeChannel::over(values[0])` -> `values[4]` (main.rs:108), the exact wiring you named. It reddened `killing_the_broker_kills_its_provider_and_the_provider_s_detached_grandchild`, but at containment.rs:693 — the HARNESS BOUND, not the recorded-input assertion. Replacing the control channel means the launch frame never arrives, so nothing spawns and the coarser failure fires first; a stream MERGE, which is what you actually described, would keep launch working while adding provider bytes to the control tape. Same lesson I learned on a different task today: a mutation has to produce the specific hazard, not merely break something.
   So I did not independently reach assertion 3 by mutation. What I CAN state from reading it: assertion 3 is exact, not merely a not-contains — it requires `Tape::consumed(&wires.control)` to equal `a_launch_frame()` byte for byte, so any extra byte fails it — and its vacuity is closed by the two assertions before it. Your account is consistent with the code and with what I observed. It is a correct distinction between two failure shapes, not a narrowing, and disclosing it was right.

=== DoD 4 IS THE BEST-CONSTRUCTED TEST I HAVE REVIEWED TODAY ===
Four ORDERED assertions, each closing a way the next could pass for the wrong reason:
(1) `would_be_obeyed_on_fd0(&hostile)` proves the hostile bytes really are a frame the control path would have obeyed — through the production decoder and accept state machine, not by assertion. A deviation fixture that is invalid at an earlier layer would make everything below unimpressive, and this closes it.
(2) `Tape::consumed(provider_out/err) == hostile` proves the bytes ENTERED the broker. Without it, "never reached control" is vacuously true of bytes that went nowhere.
(3) The DoD 4 assertion on the control path's recorded input, both directions.
(4) The run was not hijacked.
Plus the scripted `TimedOut` then `Signalled` so the session genuinely polls fd0 — a first `Signalled` would end the run before the control loop ran once, and the test would assert separation against a broker that never went looking. That is the detail most people would miss.

=== DoD 2 / RAIL 1 ===
`judge()` compares `calls.creation_time(handle)` against the recorded identity, so death is proved by the (pid, creation_time) pair. And there is a dedicated test — `the_creation_time_half_of_an_identity_is_load_bearing` (:299) — proving the second half is not decorative. A guard whose extra half is never exercised is the usual way "PID plus creation time" degrades back into PID alone.

=== DoD 3 ===
Two separately named tests, `ordinary_completion_observes_an_empty_job_without_terminating_it` (:372) and `cancel_terminates_and_then_still_observes_an_empty_job` (:396), each asserting ActiveProcesses == 0. Neither inferred from the other, exactly as rail 3 requires. Your note that mutating settle.rs reddens ONLY the completion test and leaves cancel green is the evidence those two paths really are independent.

=== DoD 6, WITH A POSITIVE CONTROL BECAUSE AN EMPTY GREP PROVES NOTHING ===
Comment-stripped grep over broker/src for CreateJobObject / AssignProcessToJobObject / CreateProcessW / ResumeThread / TerminateProcess / WaitForSingleObject: ZERO. My first positive control was mis-pathed and returned nothing, which proves nothing, so I re-ran it across the whole native tree: 6 hits in src/win32.rs, 6 in system_process.rs, 4 in system_lifecycle.rs, 3 in system_job.rs, 1 in process.rs. The command works and the Win32 authority genuinely lives in core. The 4 hits in broker/tests/session.rs are `NativeOp::CreateJobObject`-style enum variants in a fault-injection fake — precisely the false positive the architect warned about, and in tests/ rather than sources.

=== DoD 7 ===
Line counts by `grep -c ''`: frames.rs 223, descriptors.rs 222, session.rs 214, protocol.rs 205, control.rs 204, detached_spawner.rs 185 — all under 250. No binaries, no target output; `git ls-files dist/` empty. Cleanup is a `Drop` impl so it survives panic, per rail 6.

=== ONE OBSERVATION, NOT A DEFECT ===
The description names `tests/real_broker.rs`; the acceptance sweep landed as `tests/containment.rs`. Same content, better name for what it holds. Recording it only so a future reader grepping for the DoD's filename finds the explanation.

Your two self-found process leaks — Node not publishing the broker pid leaving a parked broker holding its Job for 30 minutes with nobody able to name it, and a spawner that failed to publish leaving an unreapable grandchild — are both real and both exactly the class of bug this task exists to prevent leaking into production.

  provider_bytes_that_are_a_valid_control_frame_never_reach_the_control_path ... FAILED
  panicked at broker\tests\containment.rs:468: provider bytes appeared in what the control path read
  test result: FAILED. 6 passed; 1 failed
Assertion 3 fires, and it fires BEFORE the outcome assertion, so the two assertions genuinely cover two distinct failure shapes and neither subsumes the other. containment.rs restored, `git hash-object` bffcbb78669664df683be3f3513f6766fd277a47 before and after, `git status -- packages/runner` empty.

THE LIMIT OF WHAT THIS PROVES, which the worker stated before I could and which I am recording as the finding rather than as a hedge. This is a TEST-SIDE mutation, and a test-side mutation cannot establish that a production guard catches a production defect. No code path today can put provider bytes on the control tape, so no single-token production mutation can reach assertion 3 at all. That makes it a FORWARD guard against a wiring shape that does not exist yet. For a forward guard the answerable question is narrower — "is this assertion alive or is it dead code?" — and a test-side mutation is the correct instrument for exactly that question. So: assertion 3 is proven ALIVE. Whether it guards a currently reachable defect is not proven, and cannot be today. Both halves belong in the record; the green run alone would overstate it.

This does not change the approval. DoD 4 asks that the assertion be on the control path's recorded input rather than on the absence of a crash, and it is — with exact byte equality against the launch frame, and with its vacuity closed by the two assertions before it.

TWO PROCESS ERRORS OF MY OWN FROM THIS REVIEW, recorded because I have been asking workers to disclose theirs.
1. My first DoD 6 positive control was mis-pathed and printed nothing. A silent positive control has the IDENTICAL failure mode as the absence check it exists to validate, so "nothing" is not a result in either direction — it means the control did not run. The operational fix is to require the control to print a NONZERO COUNT and treat silence as a failed run. My corrected control: broker/src ZERO, while the same comment-stripped grep hits 6 in src/win32.rs, 6 in system_process.rs, 4 in system_lifecycle.rs, 3 in system_job.rs.
2. My first attempt at the merge drill left the mutation ON DISK — a mistyped `cd` meant the `git checkout --` never executed, and only the hash comparison caught it (3fef565b against the expected bffcbb78). With a whole-tree completion hook active in a shared worktree, that is exactly how a reviewer's drill edit gets committed under someone else's task id. Restored and verified within the minute. Never trust a restore you have not hash-checked.

planningNotes.approachesConsidered:
SERIALISING THE THREE TERMINATION PATHS — REJECTED explicitly by DoD 1 and taskRail 2. 3c already proved CANCEL, fd0 EOF and instructed timeout INDIVIDUALLY with per-path call-count tables; running them one after another here adds nothing and the DoD says so outright. The race must be a genuine rendezvous (Barrier releasing three threads at once), looped enough times that a scheduling-order-dependent double-terminate surfaces rather than passing on one lucky interleaving.

PROVING DEATH BY PID — REJECTED by taskRail 1, which calls it a false green rather than a shortcut. Windows reuses PIDs, so a PID-only check can report an unrelated live process as the dead one. Both identities must be captured as (pid, creationTime) BEFORE the kill and re-checked after, which is why the cooperating binary must print creation times rather than the test inferring them later.

A SINGLE SHARED COMPLETION ASSERTION — REJECTED by DoD 3, which requires the controlled paths' ActiveProcesses==0 and the forcible-kill path's last-handle close to be asserted SEPARATELY with neither inferred from the other. taskRail 3 is the reason: last-handle close is crash safety, not success evidence, and a shared helper would let the weaker mechanism stand in for the stronger one.

"NOTHING BAD HAPPENED" FOR THE CONFUSED DEPUTY — REJECTED by DoD 4, which says the assertion is explicitly NOT the absence of a crash or an unexpected status. A broker that PARSED the provider bytes and coincidentally produced the same fd1 output would pass that. Assert on the control path's RECORDED INPUT.

A NAIVE GREP FOR THE FORBIDDEN CALLS — REJECTED, from direct experience: I specified exactly that in 3c's plan and it returns five hits, all comments, because the module docs name those calls to state the rail. Comment-strip first, and prefer asserting the delegation is present.

REUSING handle_probe.rs FOR THE GRANDCHILD — REJECTED. It is 3a's cooperating child for the descriptor absence proof and has a different output contract; a second focused binary is cleaner than overloading it, and it follows the same established pattern.

planningNotes.risks:
1. CONCURRENCY THAT IS SECRETLY SEQUENTIAL. A sleep-staggered sequence looks like a race and proves nothing; DoD 1 rejects it by name. Use a real rendezvous and loop it — a single iteration of a genuine race still frequently passes against a broken implementation.

2. DEATH PROVED BY PID ALONE. Windows PID reuse makes this a false GREEN, not merely a weak check: the assertion can resolve to an unrelated live process and report it dead. Capture (pid, creationTime) before the kill for both parent and grandchild.

3. ONE MECHANISM INFERRING THE OTHER. If the controlled path's ActiveProcesses==0 assertion is satisfied by last-handle close, the stronger guarantee silently degrades to the weaker one. DoD 3 requires both asserted separately.

4. CONFUSED-DEPUTY TEST THAT ASSERTS ABSENCE OF A CRASH. A broker that parsed the bytes and produced identical output passes it. Assert the control path's recorded input.

5. THE NAIVE GREP, which I already got wrong once on this crate. It hits comments that state the rail. Comment-strip, or assert delegation presence.

6. LEAKED PROCESSES ON A PANIC PATH. A detached grandchild that outlives a failing test is a stray process on the developer's host, and the whole point of the binary is that it is hard to kill. Use a Drop guard so cleanup runs on assertion failure, not just on success.

7. A SIBLING SUITE THAT STAYS GREEN UNDER MUTATION. DoD 5's regression method will surface a detached assertion in 3a/3b/3c work. If one does not redden, that is a finding to report, not something to route around — and as the final child this task owns noticing it.

8. COMMITTING BUILD OUTPUT OR A PROBE ARTIFACT. target/ exists in this tree and the new binary produces one.

APPROVED, all 7 DoD. Evidence: comment-36412b16322c41ad90b3c803144c5afe. Tree clean after my drill.

Not a rejection reason; verified by state at HEAD. Fifth incident from that hook today.

THE VACUITY CONTROL is the best idea here: killing_only_the_provider_leaves_its_detached_grandchild_running runs with NO broker and NO Job and REQUIRES the grandchild to survive. Without it the containment proof measures ordinary parent-child reaping and stays green forever.

DoD 4 is the best-constructed test I reviewed today: four ORDERED assertions, each closing a way the next could pass wrongly — bytes proven a real frame via the production decoder, proven CONSUMED from fd4/fd5, exact equality on the control tape, and no hijack.

DoD 2/rail 1: judge() compares creation_time, and a dedicated test proves that half load-bearing.

MY DRILL AND ITS LIMIT, reported not glossed: I mutated control values[0] -> values[4]. It reddened at containment.rs:693 — the harness BOUND, not the recorded-input assertion, because replacing the channel kills launch while a stream MERGE would not. So I did NOT independently reach that assertion. From reading it: it needs exact byte equality with the launch frame, its vacuity is closed by the two before it, and your account matches the code. Correct distinction, not a narrowing. It also confirmed your bounded await_report — failed BY NAME in 30.13s rather than hanging.

DoD 6 with a positive control: stripped grep over broker/src returns ZERO; the same grep hits 6 in src/win32.rs plus more across core.
